about: One entry per term and scope. A finding's first use of a term marks it; the page links each use to its entry, and the glossary page links each entry to every use.

terms.definition: a dated written plan for a study, fixed and hash-locked before any result is seen: the question, the data, the statistic, the controls, the forecasts and the kill conditions
terms.excludes: a plan revised after looking at the outcome, and a protocol written only for the record after the run

terms.field: research method; called a positive control in experimental science
terms.definition: data built so that the right answer is known, run through the same analysis before the real data, to show that the analysis can see the effect when it is there
terms.excludes: any check made on the real data, which cannot show what the analysis misses

terms.definition: a version of the data with the structure under test removed (for example shuffled or pooled), scored the same way as the real data, so the real score has something to beat
terms.excludes: a comparison with a different dataset or with a published number

terms.definition: the spread of scores a control gives over many random draws; its 95th percentile is the bar a real score must clear
terms.excludes: a theoretical distribution assumed rather than drawn from the data

terms.field: research method (our usage, after Popper's falsification)
terms.definition: a rule written in the preregistration that, when met, decides against the claim with no room for judgement after the run
terms.excludes: reasons found after the run for setting a result aside

terms.definition: the verdict of a run whose planted check failed or whose sample fell below its stated minimum; it says nothing for or against the claim
terms.excludes: a null result, which comes from a working instrument

terms.definition: a working test that found no effect beyond a stated bound, a forecast that failed, or an error of our own found and fixed, reported with the same weight as a positive result
terms.excludes: a void run, and a result left unpublished because it was negative

terms.definition: the pass or fail of one preregistered rule set against the run's numbers, read off by code
terms.excludes: an interpretation written after reading the numbers

terms.definition: how ready a finding is to publish: A candidate, B signal worth expanding (B* strong), C internal, D honest null worth reporting, E not reliable as it stands
terms.excludes: a measure of how large or how true an effect is

terms.definition: where a claim stands logically: lead, hypothesis, thesis, conjecture, theorem, law candidate, or killed
terms.excludes: how ready the write-up is, which the tier records

terms.field: our findings ledger, after the citators used in law (KeyCite, Shepard's)
terms.definition: what later records did to a finding: held, extended, narrowed, questioned, refuted, retracted or superseded, computed from those records and never set by hand
terms.excludes: the finding's own verdict at the time it was run

terms.definition: the append-only, dated list of every result we have recorded, numbered F1, F2 and on; corrections are added as new dated lines and old entries are never rewritten
terms.excludes: a curated list of successes

terms.definition: the closing statement of what was checked for publication, by what means, with what result and on what date; anything not checked is named as such
terms.excludes: a claim that the finding is true

terms.definition: the share of control draws scoring at or above the real score, with one added to the count and to the number of draws, so it is never zero
terms.excludes: a p value from a textbook formula that assumes a distribution

terms.definition: the range that holds the middle 95 percent of the bootstrap or control draws for a number; we report it beside the number
terms.excludes: a statement that the true value lies inside with 95 percent probability

terms.definition: the bright and dark circles seen where a curved lens rests on flat glass, made by light reflected from the two faces of the thin air gap between them, whose thickness grows with distance from the point of contact
terms.excludes: rings made by diffraction at an edge or an aperture

terms.definition: the angle between the light's path and the perpendicular to the glass; Newton's table gives it twice, once inside the glass and once in the air gap
terms.excludes: the tilt of the glass itself, which stays fixed

terms.definition: the statement that the air thickness at which a given ring appears grows as one over the cosine of the light's angle in the air gap, scaled here so that perpendicular light gives 10
terms.excludes: any rule built from the angle in the glass

terms.field: history of optics; Newton's own rule in Opticks, Book II
terms.definition: Newton's statement that the thickness goes as the secant of an angle whose sine is the first of 106 arithmetical means between the sines of incidence and refraction, counted from the bigger sine
terms.excludes: the secant law, which uses the air angle alone

terms.definition: the share of light power a thin layer reflects when every reflected and re-reflected beam inside it is summed, rather than only the first two
terms.excludes: the two-beam approximation, and absorption in the glass

terms.definition: the two directions of the light's electric field relative to the plane that holds the ray and the perpendicular to the surface: s across that plane and p within it; unpolarised light is their average
terms.excludes: circular polarisation, which this study does not model

terms.definition: the change of sign of the reflected wave at one face of the air gap and not the other, which makes the centre of the rings dark in reflected light
terms.excludes: the phase delay from the path across the gap

terms.definition: a standard table of the power in average midday daylight at each wavelength, used as the white light in this study
terms.excludes: the measured spectrum of any one day's sunlight, and Newton's own light

terms.definition: the brightness of light as the standard eye weighs it, computed by weighting power at each wavelength with the CIE 1931 2 degree observer's brightness curve
terms.excludes: hue and saturation, which the study does not score

terms.definition: a root tip of a plant enclosed by a fungus that lives with it, the fungus taking sugars from the plant and passing it water and soil nutrients; here the tuberculate root tips that Rhizopogon fungi form on Douglas-fir
terms.excludes: fungi that rot wood or cause disease, and fungal threads in the soil away from a root

terms.definition: one genetic individual of a fungus, recognised by its microsatellite profile, which may spread through the soil and colonise many root tips
terms.excludes: a species, and a single fungal thread or fruiting body

terms.definition: a network with two kinds of node, here trees and fungal genets, in which a link joins a tree to a genet found on at least one of its root tips and never joins two nodes of the same kind
terms.excludes: a network of measured flows between trees

terms.definition: the number of links a node has: the genets on one tree, the trees one genet reaches, or, in the tree-tree view, the other trees that share at least one genet with a tree
terms.excludes: the strength or direction of a link

terms.definition: a control that rewires the links of a network at random while every tree keeps its number of genets and every genet its number of trees, drawn here by the curveball algorithm 1,000 times per plot
terms.excludes: a shuffle that also changes how many links each node has

terms.definition: the share of all tree-tree links held by the top 10 percent of trees ranked by their number of tree-tree links
terms.excludes: a measure of how much a hub tree passes to others

terms.definition: the degree to which the partners of poorly linked nodes are a subset of the partners of well linked nodes, scored from 0 to 100 by the NODF index (nestedness based on overlap and decreasing fill)
terms.excludes: modules, which are groups of nodes linked mostly among themselves

terms.definition: Newman's Q: how far links fall inside groups of nodes rather than between groups, beyond what random links with the same degrees would give; here the best of 20 Louvain runs
terms.excludes: spatial clumping of samples, which can produce modules without any network structure

terms.definition: the real value minus the mean of the control draws, divided by their standard deviation; values beyond 2 in size are rare under the control
terms.excludes: a p value, and a measure of effect size in the units of the data

terms.definition: a degree distribution whose tail falls as a fixed power of the degree, so that a few nodes have very many links; a network with such a tail is called scale-free
terms.excludes: skewed distributions with an exponential tail, which also have a few well linked nodes

terms.definition: the Akaike information criterion, twice the number of fitted parameters minus twice the log-likelihood; between two models fitted to the same data the lower value is preferred, and a gap of 2 or more is the usual bar
terms.excludes: a test that one model is true

terms.definition: the correlation between the ranks of two quantities, from -1 to 1, which counts any steadily rising or falling relation and is not pulled by single extreme values
terms.excludes: the slope of a relation, and evidence of cause

terms.definition: the Spearman correlation between two quantities after the ranks of a third, here the number of root tips sampled per tree, have been regressed out of both
terms.excludes: a causal effect, and a correction that is known to be the right size

terms.definition: an interval made by recomputing a number many times on units drawn with replacement from the data, here trees, logs or inventory plots, and keeping the middle 95 percent of the results
terms.excludes: an interval that also covers doubt about the model's form

terms.definition: the apparent density of a log tissue at a sampling time divided by the same log's density of that tissue when the log was laid out in 1985
terms.excludes: mass loss and carbon loss, which also count the volume a log loses as it fragments

terms.definition: the constant k in the single-exponential model, the fraction of remaining density lost per year; a half-life is the natural log of 2 divided by k
terms.excludes: a rate measured from mass, and the rate in the first years of a lag model

terms.definition: the forecast that a later sampling will show the same mean relative density as the last sampling used for fitting, here year 16
terms.excludes: a forecast from a fitted decay curve

terms.definition: one minus the mean absolute error of a model's forecast divided by the mean absolute error of a baseline on the same held-out logs; 0 means no better than the baseline and 1 means perfect
terms.excludes: a score on the logs used to fit the model

terms.definition: a model that gives the log odds of a yes-or-no outcome, here recorded wind damage, as a weighted sum of the features; here fitted with an L2 penalty on standardised features
terms.excludes: a model of how much damage a tree has

terms.definition: the factor by which the odds of the outcome change when a feature rises by one standard deviation and the other features stay fixed; 1 means no change
terms.excludes: a ratio of probabilities, and a causal effect

terms.definition: tree height divided by stem diameter at breast height, both in the same units
terms.excludes: the height-to-diameter ratio measured at the base of the stem

terms.definition: the area under the ROC curve: the chance that a randomly chosen damaged tree is ranked above a randomly chosen undamaged one, with 0.5 for guessing
terms.excludes: how close the predicted probabilities are to the observed rates

terms.definition: one minus the Brier score of a model divided by the Brier score of always forecasting the base rate, where the Brier score is the mean squared gap between a probability and the outcome coded 0 or 1
terms.excludes: a ranking measure such as AUC, which ignores whether the probabilities are right in size

terms.definition: how far a person's mood at one prompt predicts their mood at the next, measured as the lag-one correlation of their own mood series
terms.excludes: average mood, how much mood varies, and any claim about what causes the carryover

terms.definition: a study design in which people answer short questions on a phone several times a day, so that mood is recorded close to the moment it is felt
terms.excludes: one-off questionnaires and recall of past weeks

terms.definition: two adjacent prompts on the same study day, the earlier one called the lead; a missed prompt or a night breaks the pair
terms.excludes: pairs that cross a night or skip a prompt

terms.definition: a lead prompt whose mood sits at least 1.5 of the person's own standard deviations from the person's own mean
terms.excludes: deviations judged against other people or against a population norm

terms.definition: the median, over a person's spikes, of the share of each spike's distance from the person's mean that has gone by the next prompt, with 1 meaning back at the mean and 0 meaning no change
terms.excludes: recovery measured in clock time, and recovery after events that did not produce a spike

terms.definition: a series in which each value is the mean plus a fixed fraction of the previous value's distance from the mean, plus fresh random noise; the fraction is the single parameter
terms.excludes: models with separate rates for small and large deviations, and models with measurement noise on top

terms.definition: the correlation coefficient between two quantities measured on the same units, from -1 through 0 for no linear relation to 1
terms.excludes: non-linear relations and any statement about cause

terms.definition: an interval found by drawing people with replacement many times, recomputing the statistic each time, and taking the middle of the resulting spread
terms.excludes: resampling of single prompts, which would treat one person's prompts as independent

terms.definition: the correlation across people between a measure computed on one half of each person's data and the same measure on the other half; here the halves are odd and even study days
terms.excludes: test-retest reliability over months, and the validity of the measure

terms.definition: a model that explains the correlations among several measured indicators by a smaller number of unseen common factors, fitted by maximum likelihood
terms.excludes: exploratory searches for the number of factors, and models of change over time

terms.definition: the Bayesian information criterion, a fit score that charges each extra parameter a penalty growing with sample size; the lower value is preferred
terms.excludes: a test of whether either model is true

terms.definition: the downward bias of a lag-one correlation estimated from a short series, about (1 + 3 phi)/n for a series of n values with true value phi (Kendall 1954)
terms.excludes: bias from measurement noise, which is a separate attenuation

terms.definition: the shrinking of an observed correlation toward zero when the measures that enter it are noisy
terms.excludes: a true weak relation between the underlying quantities

terms.definition: a test of whether a model with more free parameters fits nested data better than a simpler model, using the drop in the chi-square fit statistic against its degrees of freedom
terms.excludes: comparisons of models that are not nested

terms.definition: a score for probability forecasts on which a forecaster does best in expectation by stating their true belief
terms.excludes: scores that pay for shading a forecast toward some answer, and any rule for which questions to answer

terms.definition: the squared difference between the stated probabilities and the outcomes, here summed over the answer options in the GJP form so it runs from 0 to 2; lower is better
terms.excludes: questions left unanswered, which it does not score

terms.definition: prediction with a reject option, where a system answers only the inputs it ranks most likely to be right and declines the rest
terms.excludes: how the kept answers are produced

terms.definition: the error on kept items against the share kept; here risk is the mean Brier score of kept forecasts and coverage the share kept
terms.excludes: any score for the forecasts withheld

terms.definition: pushing a probability away from 50 percent by multiplying its log-odds by a factor a, with a below 1 pulling it inward instead
terms.excludes: changing which side a forecast leans to

terms.definition: the Creative Commons public domain dedication, under which anyone may reuse the work for any purpose without permission
terms.excludes: a licence condition requiring citation, which stays a scholarly courtesy

terms.definition: a market in which people trade contracts that pay on an outcome, with the price read as a probability
terms.excludes: the individual survey forecasts analysed in this paper

terms.definition: a hash function that turns a file into a 64-character fingerprint which changes if any byte changes; a recorded hash shows the file was not altered after it was taken
terms.excludes: encryption, because the hash keeps nothing secret and cannot be turned back into the file

terms.definition: a question the tournament cancelled without scoring, so no forecast on it has an outcome
terms.excludes: a void verdict in our sense, which concerns a failed planted check or a sample below its minimum

terms.definition: a team made up of forecasters drawn from the top performers of the previous tournament year (condition 5)
terms.excludes: ordinary teams (condition 4), formed without selection on past accuracy

terms.definition: a closed question that was open during a forecaster's active window in a year and that they never answered, inferred from the data
terms.excludes: questions outside the active window, and any recorded decision to decline, which the data do not hold

terms.definition: a forecaster's mean, over the questions they answered, of their first-forecast Brier score minus the median first-forecast Brier score on that question; lower is better
terms.excludes: the difficulty of the question, which subtracting the median removes

terms.definition: one person's forecasts within one tournament year, the unit for skip rate and relative score
terms.excludes: pooling of different people, and pooling one person's years

terms.definition: a group of units alike on the matched variables, here year and twentieth of forecast count, inside which a statistic is computed before averaging
terms.excludes: control for variables that were not matched

terms.definition: the correlation between the ranks of two quantities, from -1 to +1, which reads any steady rise or fall
terms.excludes: the shape of the relation and the pull of outliers on the raw values

terms.definition: recomputing a number many times on data resampled with replacement, here within strata or over questions, to see how much it varies
terms.excludes: an interval from a textbook formula that assumes a distribution

terms.definition: for a probability p, the natural log of p divided by 1 minus p; 0 at 50 percent and unbounded toward certainty
terms.excludes: any information beyond the probability, of which it is a rescaling

terms.definition: the drop in Brier score from extremising, with the factor fitted on one half of the questions and scored on the other half
terms.excludes: the in-sample improvement any fitted factor gives on the data it was fitted to

terms.definition: a prediction for each item made from a fit on the other folds only
terms.excludes: any use of the item's own outcome to predict it

terms.definition: the mean risk over coverages from 10 to 100 percent in steps of 5, one number for a whole filter; lower is better
terms.excludes: coverages below 10 percent

terms.definition: a test of an effect already known to be present, which the instrument must detect for its other readings to be trusted
terms.excludes: a shuffle control, which removes an effect instead

terms.definition: the correlation between one person's value in one year and the same person's value in the next, a measure of how stable the quantity is
terms.excludes: change caused by anything the person did between the two years

terms.definition: the gap between stated probability and hit rate, averaged over probability bins and weighted by bin size; folded here by taking each forecast on the side it leans to
terms.excludes: how informative forecasts are, since a forecast of the base rate every time can score zero

terms.definition: two rating scales for emotion: arousal runs from calm to excited and valence from unpleasant to pleasant; in DEAM each is a nine-point scale averaged over crowd raters
terms.excludes: named emotions such as sadness or nostalgia, which the ratings place only as points on the two scales

terms.definition: the emotion a listener judges the music to express, as opposed to the emotion the listener feels
terms.excludes: felt or induced emotion, physiological response and any change in mood or symptoms

terms.definition: for each note onset found in the energy envelope, the time constant of the envelope's decay from its peak to the next minimum, with the median taken over onsets; it follows whichever of the note's own decay and the room's decay is slower
terms.excludes: the reverberation time of the room on its own, which this measure cannot separate in dense music

terms.definition: the slope of log power against log frequency between 110 Hz and 5.5 kHz; a more negative slope means energy leans toward low frequencies and the sound is darker
terms.excludes: pitch, loudness and the shape of the spectrum beyond its overall tilt

terms.definition: the correlation between two quantities after each has had the linear effect of a set of control variables removed by least squares
terms.excludes: a causal effect, and any non-linear dependence on the controls

terms.definition: data kept apart from everything that was fitted or standardised, here every clip by 30 percent of the artists, so that a result on it is a check on new material
terms.excludes: data used to fit the model, choose a threshold or compute a scaling

terms.definition: the share of variance in the test outcome explained by a model fitted on training data with the added measures, minus the same share for the model without them
terms.excludes: the in-sample R2 of a fit, which can only grow as variables are added

terms.definition: a bootstrap that resamples whole groups, here artists with all their clips, so that clips by one artist count as one draw
terms.excludes: a bootstrap over single clips, which treats one artist's clips as independent

terms.definition: the best held-out score any model could reach on a target, given how far repeated measurements of that same target disagree; it is estimated from the data's own repeats
terms.excludes: the best score reached so far by any model, and a bound set by missing variables

terms.definition: a model's score on cases kept apart from fitting: R2 for numbers, the area under the ROC curve for yes-or-no outcomes, and accuracy for triplet choices
terms.excludes: the score on the data used to fit the model

terms.definition: the area under the ROC curve: the chance that a randomly chosen positive case is ranked above a randomly chosen negative one, with 0.5 for guessing
terms.excludes: accuracy at any one threshold

terms.definition: least squares with a penalty on the size of the coefficients, chosen by leave-one-out error, so that many variables can be fitted without chasing noise
terms.excludes: non-linear models such as boosted trees or neural networks

terms.definition: held-out skill above chance divided by the noise ceiling above chance; 1 means the model scores as well as the measurements allow
terms.excludes: the raw skill, which is not comparable across targets

terms.definition: the curve s(k) = a k / (k + h) fitted to skill above chance against the number of variables k, where a is the level it approaches
terms.excludes: a forecast of skill with variables not in the dataset

terms.definition: the mean squared difference between a probability forecast and the outcome coded 0 or 1; lower is better
terms.excludes: measures that score only whether the most likely outcome happened

terms.definition: the correlation between scores computed on two halves of the same items, here a forecaster's accuracy on the odd and the even questions
terms.excludes: agreement between different people or different occasions

terms.definition: two items meant to measure the same thing, answered at the same time; their correlation estimates reliability, here happy and cheerful at the same beep
terms.excludes: the same item repeated later, which also picks up real change

terms.definition: a variable of a different kind from the base set, named for each target before the run: past behaviour of the same unit, or a human rating of a related quantity
terms.excludes: one more variable of the kind already in the base set

terms.definition: the time until a forecast from a slightly wrong starting state differs from the truth by more than a set tolerance; in a chaotic system it grows with the logarithm of the starting precision
terms.excludes: errors from a wrong model, which the toy does not have

terms.definition: a published forecast that the forecast population reads and reacts to, so that publishing it changes the outcome it predicts
terms.excludes: a forecast kept private from the people it describes

terms.definition: a 28-item adult self-report questionnaire about childhood experiences, scored as five subscales (emotional abuse, physical abuse, sexual abuse, emotional neglect, physical neglect) of 5 to 25 each and a total of 25 to 125, plus minimisation items that flag denial
terms.excludes: records of maltreatment from the time it happened, and clinical diagnosis

terms.definition: the correlation over time between the blood-oxygen signals of two brain regions while a person lies in the scanner with no task
terms.excludes: anatomical connections, activity evoked by a task, and the direction of any influence between regions

terms.definition: a pair of almond-shaped structures deep in the temporal lobes, one per hemisphere, involved in detecting threat and in emotional learning
terms.excludes: its separate subnuclei, which the anatomical masks here do not distinguish

terms.definition: the lower middle part of the frontal lobe, linked to the regulation of emotional responses; here defined by the Harvard-Oxford label Frontal Medial Cortex
terms.excludes: functional definitions from a task, and the dorsal and lateral prefrontal cortex

terms.definition: a probabilistic atlas of cortical and subcortical regions in standard brain space; at a 50 percent threshold a voxel belongs to a region when at least half of the reference brains placed it there
terms.excludes: regions drawn from each participant's own anatomy or from functional data

terms.definition: an open preprocessing pipeline for functional MRI that corrects head motion and distortion, aligns images to a standard brain space and writes nuisance signals for later cleaning
terms.excludes: the denoising and statistics that follow, which were run by our own code

terms.definition: a summary of how far the head moved between two consecutive brain volumes, in millimetres, from the six rigid-body motion parameters
terms.excludes: motion within a single volume

terms.definition: dropping single brain volumes whose head motion exceeds a threshold before connectivity is computed
terms.excludes: dropping whole runs or whole participants, which follow separate rules

terms.definition: anatomical component correction: the main components of the signal in white matter and cerebrospinal fluid, where little neural signal is expected, are regressed out as noise
terms.excludes: global signal regression, which removes the mean of the whole brain

terms.definition: removing the average signal of the whole brain from every region before connectivity is computed
terms.excludes: aCompCor and motion regression, which remove other nuisance signals

terms.definition: the transform z = artanh(r) of a correlation, which makes its sampling spread close to normal so that correlations can be averaged and given intervals
terms.excludes: any change to the sign or ranking of correlations

terms.definition: the correlation between two quantities after the linear effect of a set of covariates has been removed from both
terms.excludes: adjustment for covariates that were not measured, and any statement about cause

terms.definition: the size of effect, fixed before the data are seen, below which an effect is treated as too small to matter for the decision at hand; here a correlation of 0.20 in size
terms.excludes: a claim that smaller effects are zero

terms.definition: a test that supports the absence of a meaningful effect when the 90 percent interval of the estimate lies wholly inside the band set by the smallest effect of interest, which is the same as rejecting both edges of the band at the 5 percent level
terms.excludes: a test of whether the effect is exactly zero

terms.definition: a step-down adjustment of p values across a family of tests that keeps the chance of any false positive in the family at the stated level
terms.excludes: adjustment for analyses outside the declared family, such as the exploratory sensitivity checks

terms.definition: the chance that a test detects an effect of a stated size, given the sample size and the threshold for significance
terms.excludes: the chance that a detected effect is real

terms.definition: a dated, reasoned change to a preregistered plan, written into the plan's log, with the point in the study at which it was decided
terms.excludes: a silent change to the analysis

terms.definition: a test of a known effect run through the same pipeline, to show that the pipeline can find an effect of the expected kind
terms.excludes: shuffled controls, which show what no effect looks like

terms.field: psychology and stress biology, here applied to trees
terms.definition: the idea that a moderate earlier stress leaves an organism better able to cope with a later, harder one; here, that a tree which lived through a moderate drought loses less growth to a later severe drought
terms.excludes: recovery from the same drought, and any gain that follows only from how the growth indices are computed

terms.definition: growth that stays below its expected level for one or more years after a drought ends
terms.excludes: the loss of growth in the drought year itself

terms.definition: one yearly ring-width index for a site, made by removing each tree's age trend and averaging the trees, scaled so that an ordinary year is near 1
terms.excludes: raw ring widths of single trees, and density or isotope records

terms.definition: a monthly index of soil-moisture supply against demand built from temperature and precipitation; 0 is normal, -2 is moderate drought and -3 or lower is severe drought
terms.excludes: a direct measurement of soil water, and drought indices built on precipitation alone

terms.definition: a version of the Palmer index whose constants are fitted to each location's own climate, so that the thresholds mean similar rarity everywhere; here taken from the CRU TS gridded product at 0.5 degree
terms.excludes: the original Palmer index with fixed constants, and station measurements

terms.definition: one of the regions into which NOAA splits the contiguous United States for climate records, each with one averaged monthly series per variable
terms.excludes: a single weather station, and a regular grid cell

terms.definition: three ratios of ring growth around a drought year: resistance is the drought-year growth over the mean of the three years before, recovery is the mean of the three years after over the drought-year growth, and resilience is the mean after over the mean before
terms.excludes: measures of tree death, and growth responses that unfold over more than three years

terms.definition: one free constant per site (or species) and one per calendar year in a regression, so that differences between sites and between years cannot be mistaken for the effect of the variable under test
terms.excludes: random effects, which treat those constants as draws from one distribution

terms.definition: standard errors computed so that events in the same climate division may be correlated with each other, which widens the interval when they are
terms.excludes: ordinary standard errors that treat every event as independent

terms.definition: a control in which each drought record is moved in time by a random offset of 20 years or more, with the end wrapped round to the start, and the events rebuilt; it keeps each record's own pattern of droughts and breaks its timing against the rings
terms.excludes: shuffling single years, which also destroys the drought record's own pattern

terms.definition: a control in which the prior-drought labels are shuffled among each site's own events, keeping every drought date in place
terms.excludes: a null that moves the droughts themselves

terms.definition: the same test run with the exposure window placed after the event, years 5 to 12 later, where no causal effect is possible, so that any effect found there points to a flaw in the design
terms.excludes: a control on the outcome data

terms.definition: a rule that adjusts a set of p values so that, among the tests called significant, the expected share of false calls stays at or below a chosen rate, here 0.05; the adjusted value is called q
terms.excludes: the stricter Bonferroni rule, which bounds the chance of any false call

terms.definition: a test for a rise-then-fall shape that fits one straight line on each side of a data-chosen break point and asks whether the first rises and the second falls, both significantly
terms.excludes: a quadratic fit, which can report a peak where none exists

terms.definition: how a series' variance is spread over frequencies, from slow swings to fast jitter
terms.excludes: the timing or phase of the swings, which the spectrum does not record

terms.field: signal processing (speech coding) and the theory of stationary processes
terms.definition: the geometric mean of a power spectrum divided by its arithmetic mean; it is 1 for white noise and near 0 when a few frequencies hold most of the variance
terms.excludes: flatness of the series itself in time, and measures that use the spectrum's entropy instead of its geometric mean

terms.field: the theory of weakly stationary processes
terms.definition: the smallest one-step error variance any linear predictor can reach on a weakly stationary series, equal to the exponential of the average log spectrum; one minus the flatness is therefore the most variance a linear one-step forecast can remove
terms.excludes: nonlinear predictors on non-Gaussian series, multi-step forecasts, and series whose statistics drift over time

terms.definition: a series whose mean and autocovariance do not change over time
terms.excludes: series with trends, level shifts or drifting variance, such as a machine whose load changes between the halves

terms.definition: the squared Fourier transform of a series after its ends are faded with a Hann window, used as a raw estimate of the power spectrum at each Fourier frequency
terms.excludes: smoothed or averaged spectrum estimates such as Welch's method, which we report only as secondaries

terms.definition: a linear forecast of the next value from a weighted sum of the last p values, with the weights fitted by least squares; p is the order
terms.excludes: models with moving-average terms, external inputs or nonlinear terms

terms.definition: the Akaike information criterion, a fit score that adds a penalty of two per fitted parameter, used here to choose the autoregressive order
terms.excludes: choice by held-out error, which would use the test half

terms.definition: one minus the mean squared error of one-step-ahead forecasts on the test half, divided by the test half's variance; 0 matches forecasting the mean and 1 is perfect
terms.excludes: skill at longer horizons and skill measured on the data used to fit the model

terms.definition: a copy of a series with the same power spectrum and random Fourier phases, so it keeps the autocorrelation and is Gaussian and stationary by construction

terms.definition: a tendency of a method's update rule to pull candidates toward the centre of the search box, which helps on any function whose minimum happens to sit there
terms.excludes: good performance that survives when the minimum is moved

terms.definition: the version of each test function whose minimum is moved to a random point with every coordinate between -70 and 70 and whose axes are turned by a random rotation, the same for every method within one repeat
terms.excludes: the unshifted arm, with the minimum at the centre and the axes aligned

terms.definition: each method's rank on each function by median final error, averaged over the seven functions; 1 is best and 10 is worst
terms.excludes: how large the differences in error are

terms.definition: a factor of ten; a change of one decade in error is a change of one in its base-10 logarithm
terms.excludes: a difference on a linear scale

terms.definition: for one method, the median over the seven functions of how many decades its median error grows when the function moves from the unshifted arm to the shifted arm
terms.excludes: effects of the rotation alone, which the design does not separate from the shift

terms.definition: shuffling which method name goes with which rank within each function, 2,000 times, to see how large a gap between the two groups' mean ranks arises by chance
terms.excludes: uncertainty from the random repeats of each run

terms.field: optimisation theory, after Wolpert and Macready
terms.definition: the result that, averaged over all possible functions, every search method that never revisits a point does equally well, so any advantage on one class of functions is paid for on another
terms.excludes: claims about any one class of functions, such as the test functions here

terms.definition: a rank-based test of whether several groups of numbers come from the same distribution
terms.excludes: a test of which group is better

terms.definition: a dummy method that only samples points within a tiny distance of the centre of the box, so it solves any function whose minimum sits there and nothing else
terms.excludes: any real optimiser

terms.definition: a product that costs its maker something and benefits others nearby, such as an enzyme or iron-scavenging molecule a microbe releases into its surroundings
terms.excludes: products the maker keeps for itself

terms.definition: a producer pays a cost to make the public good; a cheater makes none and still gains from the goods of producers near it
terms.excludes: any intention on either side; the words name two fixed strategies

terms.definition: a square grid whose opposite edges are joined, so every cell has the same number of neighbours and there is no border
terms.excludes: grids with edges, where border cells have fewer neighbours

terms.definition: the update rule in which a cell's next occupant is copied from a parent drawn with chance in proportion to the parent's fitness, here among the 3 by 3 window around the cell including the cell itself
terms.excludes: other update rules, such as death followed by birth from neighbours only, or imitation of the best neighbour

terms.definition: every cell of the grid is replaced at once in each generation, from the fitnesses of the previous generation
terms.excludes: asynchronous updating, where one cell at a time is replaced

terms.definition: the square of cells over which one producer's goods are spread, 3 by 3 at range 1 and 5 by 5 at range 2
terms.excludes: the 3 by 3 window from which parents are drawn, which stays fixed

terms.definition: the part of a producer's own goods that returns to the producer itself; with a 3 by 3 box a producer keeps a ninth of what it makes
terms.excludes: benefit from the goods of other producers, including relatives

terms.definition: the benefit b that one producer's goods give in total divided by the cost c it pays, written b/c
terms.excludes: the net payoff to any one cell, which also depends on its neighbours

terms.definition: the version of the model in which every cell gains from the producer share of the whole population and parents are drawn from the whole population, so neighbours mean nothing
terms.excludes: any spatial structure

terms.definition: the version of the model in which all positions are shuffled at random before each generation and the local rules then apply, so neighbours are strangers
terms.excludes: the clustering of relatives that the local arm allows

terms.definition: an exact formula for next generation's producer share in the mixed arm, used here as a known answer the simulation must match
terms.excludes: the local and shuffled arms, which have no such formula

terms.field: social evolution, after Taylor and after Griffin and colleagues
terms.definition: competition for space or resources among neighbours, which, when neighbours are relatives, can cancel the benefit that helping relatives brings
terms.excludes: competition spread over the whole population

terms.definition: the share of producers in the grid at the end of a run, averaged over the replicate runs; a run stops early when one type takes the whole grid
terms.excludes: the share of runs in which producers survived

terms.field: particle physics and quantum gravity phenomenology
terms.definition: any departure from the rule of special relativity that every observer measures the same speed of light; the form tested here is a speed of light in vacuum that changes with photon energy
terms.excludes: the slowing of light in a medium such as glass or plasma, which is ordinary optics

terms.definition: the photon energy at which a speed change that grows in proportion to energy would reach the full speed of light; a lower limit on it is the usual way to state a time-of-flight bound
terms.excludes: the quadratic scale, for a speed change that grows with the square of energy, which this paper does not bound

terms.definition: the energy built from the constant of gravitation, Planck's constant and the speed of light, about 1.22e19 GeV; many quantum-gravity models expect new effects near it
terms.excludes: any energy reached by a particle accelerator, which is about fifteen powers of ten lower

terms.definition: the dependence of a wave's speed on its frequency or energy, written as a relation between frequency and wavenumber
terms.excludes: a delay that is the same at every energy, such as a fixed travel time

terms.definition: resampling the data with replacement many times and recomputing the estimate each time, so that the spread of the recomputed values gives an interval for it
terms.excludes: an interval taken from a formula that assumes a distribution

terms.definition: the speed at which a packet of waves, and the energy it carries, moves; it equals the slope of frequency against wavenumber
terms.excludes: the phase velocity, the speed of a single crest, which can differ from it

terms.definition: the frequency of small waves in a uniform condensate: equal to the sound speed times the wavenumber at long wavelength and rising faster, towards the free-particle law, at wavelengths near the healing length
terms.excludes: sound in an ordinary gas or solid, whose dispersion is set by other physics

terms.definition: the length below which a condensate's density cannot change smoothly; waves shorter than it stop behaving like sound
terms.excludes: the wavelength of any particular wave

terms.definition: the place in a moving fluid where the flow speed equals the sound speed, so that sound travelling against the flow cannot get out; it mimics the horizon of a black hole
terms.excludes: a gravitational horizon, and any place where the flow is slower than sound

terms.definition: the slope of the flow speed at the acoustic horizon; it sets how fast a trapped wave's wavelength is stretched
terms.excludes: the pull of gravity at a planet's surface

terms.definition: the On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences, a public database of number sequences in which each entry carries the first terms, formulas, comments and links contributed by many people
terms.excludes: a peer-reviewed journal; a line in an entry is a contribution, and a conjecture line in it carries no proof

terms.definition: a text file stored beside an OEIS entry that lists the sequence's index and term pairs much further than the entry's own data section, often to thousands of terms
terms.excludes: the entry's data section, which holds only the first few dozen terms

terms.definition: a comment or formula line in an OEIS entry that states an equation for the sequence and labels it a conjecture; most were found by fitting the terms then known
terms.excludes: a line marked as proved, and a statement with no equation

terms.definition: an equation that gives each term of a sequence as a fixed weighted sum of a set number of earlier terms, possibly with terms in n; here with integer coefficients
terms.excludes: an equation with a product of earlier terms, and an equation with coefficients that are not integers

terms.definition: a single case where a general statement is false; one is enough to refute a conjecture
terms.excludes: a term that disagrees because the data are wrong

terms.definition: a rule that turns each line into a syntax tree and accepts it only if every part is on a fixed list: integers, n, the terms a(n-k), addition, subtraction, multiplication and powers
terms.excludes: any line that needs division, sums, named functions or words to state

terms.definition: the list from which a sample is drawn; a result describes the frame, so a change of frame changes what the result is about
terms.excludes: the sample itself

terms.definition: a dated, recorded change from the preregistered plan, stated with its reason and with what had been seen when it was made
terms.excludes: a change made silently, and a change made after seeing the outcome it would affect without saying so

terms.definition: a 95 percent interval for a proportion, found by inverting the score test; it stays inside 0 to 1 and behaves well when the count is small or near zero
terms.excludes: the simple interval of the proportion plus or minus 1.96 standard errors, which fails near zero

terms.definition: any formula that places a system's planets at distances or periods growing by a near-constant ratio from one planet to the next, here fitted in three forms to the log of orbital period
terms.excludes: a physical model of how planets form or migrate

terms.definition: the pattern, reported from Kepler data, that planets inside one system tend to be alike in size and in the ratios between neighbouring periods
terms.excludes: a rule for the order of the gaps, and any likeness between planets of different systems

terms.definition: dropping one interior planet, fitting the rule to the others and comparing the predicted period with the true one, repeated for every interior planet
terms.excludes: scoring a planet with a fit that has already seen it

terms.definition: a hash function that turns a file into a 64-character fingerprint which changes if any byte of the file changes; a recorded hash shows the file was not edited after it was taken
terms.excludes: encryption, because the hash keeps nothing secret and cannot be turned back into the file

terms.definition: each system rebuilt from its own innermost period and its own gaps in log period, put in a random order, and scored with the same form and freedom as the real system
terms.excludes: gaps borrowed from other systems, which the pooled-gap control uses

terms.definition: each system rebuilt from gaps in log period drawn at random from all systems' gaps, and scored with the same form and freedom as the real system
terms.excludes: planets or gaps from outside the 122 systems in the sample

terms.field: our usage, fixed in the preregistration
terms.definition: the verdict that a Titius-Bode form beats the order-shuffle control's 95th percentile and predicts dropped planets better than the neighbour baseline
terms.excludes: regularity that similar gaps alone produce, which beats only the pooled-gap control

terms.definition: the Table Access Protocol of the International Virtual Observatory Alliance, the standard query interface through which astronomical archives return table rows
terms.excludes: any selection or cleaning of the rows, which the query itself sets

terms.definition: a catalogue field set to 1 when a planet's existence or confirmation has been questioned in the published literature and 0 otherwise
terms.excludes: independent confirmation, which a flag of 0 does not give

terms.definition: a search that finds planets by the small dip in a star's light as a planet crosses its disc, which favours short periods and orbits seen close to edge-on
terms.excludes: planets found only by other methods, such as radial velocity or direct imaging

terms.definition: the square root of the mean squared difference between fitted and observed log period across a system's planets, a measure of scatter about the fit
terms.excludes: any offset or trend the fit has already absorbed into its parameters

terms.definition: for two numbers, the square root of their product, which is the plain average taken on a log scale; here the neighbour baseline for a dropped planet's period
terms.excludes: the ordinary average of the two periods, which is larger whenever they differ

terms.definition: the probability that a classifier gives a randomly chosen positive case a higher score than a randomly chosen negative case; 0.5 is chance and 1 is perfect separation
terms.excludes: accuracy at one threshold, and any statement about how well the scores are calibrated as probabilities

terms.definition: fixed-length stretches cut from a recording at a step shorter than their length, so that neighbouring windows share samples; here 60 s windows every 15 s share 75 percent of their samples
terms.excludes: windows cut end to end with no shared samples

terms.field: machine learning evaluation; called record-wise cross-validation in the clinical literature
terms.definition: assigning windows to training and test sets at random, so that windows from the same person and the same recording block fall on both sides
terms.excludes: any split that keeps all of one person's data on one side

terms.field: machine learning evaluation; called subject-wise cross-validation
terms.definition: training on all people but one and scoring on the one left out, repeated so that each person is held out once
terms.excludes: a test on people from another study, lab or protocol

terms.definition: the AUC computed on one held-out person's windows alone, then averaged over people; it asks whether the classifier ranks that person's stress windows above their other windows
terms.excludes: the global AUC, which pools all held-out windows and also rewards separating people from each other

terms.definition: a classifier that averages many decision trees, each grown on a resampled copy of the training data with a random subset of features tried at each split; here 100 trees with at least 3 windows per leaf
terms.excludes: any model tuned on the test person

terms.definition: a classifier that models the log odds of the positive class as a weighted sum of the features; here on standardised features with an L2 (ridge) penalty at strength C = 1
terms.excludes: interactions between features, which it does not model unless they are added by hand

terms.definition: a laboratory stressor in which a person prepares and gives a short public talk and then does mental arithmetic aloud in front of an evaluating panel
terms.excludes: daily stress, chronic stress and trauma

terms.definition: a short form of the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory in which a person rates six statements about how they feel at that moment; positive items are reverse scored so that a higher total means more anxiety
terms.excludes: a clinical diagnosis, and anxiety as a lasting trait

terms.definition: the electrical conductance of the skin, which rises with sweat gland activity under sympathetic nervous control
terms.excludes: a direct reading of emotion; temperature and movement also change it

terms.definition: a fixed amount added to one feature in every stress window of every person in planted data, in the same direction for all, so that a classifier tested on a new person has something real to find
terms.excludes: the per-person, per-block offsets, which point in a random direction and carry nothing from one person to the next

terms.definition: the AUC a perfect reader of the one shifted feature could reach when the stress and non-stress values of that feature are normal with a variance of 1.09 each (a block offset of variance 1 plus window noise of variance 0.09)
terms.excludes: the effect of the 19 features that carry no shift, and of the small number of people

terms.definition: a rule that adjusts a set of p values so that, among the tests called significant, the expected share of false discoveries stays at or below a chosen level q
terms.excludes: control of the chance of even one false discovery, which is a stricter rule

terms.definition: the correlation between the ranks of two quantities; it runs from -1 to 1 and measures how well one quantity's order follows the other's, whatever the shape of the relation
terms.excludes: the size of the change, and any causal direction

terms.definition: redrawing people with replacement, 2,000 times, and recomputing the mean of the per-person scores each time; the middle 95 percent of those means is the interval
terms.excludes: redrawing single windows, which would treat one person's many windows as many independent people

terms.definition: an experiment in which a person observes a random outcome in private, such as a die roll or coin toss, reports it, and is paid by the report, so a lie pays and cannot be caught for any one person; lying shows only in the distribution of many reports
terms.excludes: tasks where the experimenter can see each person's true outcome

terms.field: experimental economics; the measure Abeler, Nosenzo and Raymond report, computed here by our own code
terms.definition: the mean report of a treatment after the outcomes are mapped evenly onto -1 for the lowest-paying report and +1 for the highest, so honest reporting gives 0 in expectation and everyone claiming the top gives 1; here averaged over treatments without weights
terms.excludes: a share of liars, which the mean alone does not give

terms.definition: minus the average natural log of the probability a model gave to each report that was made; lower is better, and the difference between two models in nats per report is how much better one predicts each report
terms.excludes: an accuracy count, which ignores how much probability a model gave to what happened

terms.definition: papers kept out of all fitting, chosen by a hash of the citation (30 percent of papers), on which every model is scored once; all treatments from one paper fall on the same side
terms.excludes: a split by treatment or subject, which would let one paper's design appear in both fitting and scoring

terms.definition: fitting a model's parameters by choosing the values that make the observed data most probable under the model
terms.excludes: choosing parameters by hand or by fit to the test data

terms.definition: a parameter that mixes a share of uniformly random reports into a model's prediction, standing for mistakes and inattention; in these models it is the only source of downward lies
terms.excludes: a preference, since the tremble does not depend on payoffs

terms.definition: the parameter epsilon in a stakes factor (G/5) to the power 1 minus epsilon, where G is the money at stake; at epsilon 1 the size of the payment has no effect on reports, and at 0 the pull to lie grows in proportion to the payment
terms.excludes: the effect of payment on whether people take part

terms.definition: a report distribution that, when used to compute how honest each report looks, leads people to make the same distribution of reports; found here by repeated damped updates starting from honest reporting
terms.excludes: a guarantee that the fixed point found is the only one

terms.field: experimental economics, after Fischbacher and Föllmi-Heusi
terms.definition: a split of a report distribution into honest reporters, read as the number of outcomes times the share reporting the lowest outcome, maximal liars, the excess at the top over the honest share, and partial liars, the rest
terms.excludes: an observation of any person's lie; it assumes the true outcomes are uniform and that no one lies downward on purpose

terms.field: forecast verification, where it is called climatology
terms.definition: a forecast that gives each held-out treatment the average report distribution of training treatments with the same number of outcomes
terms.excludes: any theory of why people report as they do

terms.definition: a test that sums each held-out paper's difference in log loss between two models, then flips the sign of each paper's difference at random 5,000 times to see how often a sum as large arises with no true difference
terms.excludes: a test that treats subjects within one paper as independent

terms.definition: a rule that adjusts a set of p values so that, among the tests called significant, the expected share of false calls stays at or below a chosen rate q, here 0.05
terms.excludes: the stricter Bonferroni rule, which bounds the chance of any false call

terms.definition: an interval made by recomputing a statistic 2,000 times on held-out papers drawn with replacement, so subjects from one paper stay together
terms.excludes: resampling single subjects as if they were independent

terms.definition: a charged particle from space, a proton or heavier nucleus, arriving with an energy above about 1e18 electronvolts; it is recorded through the shower of secondary particles it makes in the atmosphere
terms.excludes: photons and neutrinos, and the far more common cosmic rays of lower energy

terms.definition: an exaelectronvolt, 1e18 electronvolts, or 1e9 GeV, carried by a single particle
terms.excludes: the total energy of the shower in a detector, which is spread over many secondary particles

terms.definition: the distance between neighbouring points of a grid on which space is modelled; on a grid, waves shorter than about twice the spacing cannot exist and the speed of a wave depends on its direction
terms.excludes: the Planck length, which is a scale built from constants and not a measured grid

terms.definition: the simplest pattern on a sphere with the symmetry of a cube: here x^4 + y^4 + z^4 minus its average, largest along the six cube axes and smallest along the eight diagonals
terms.excludes: a dipole, a single hot spot, or any pattern that a rotation of the cube by a right angle would change

terms.definition: how much of each part of the sky a detector watched over time; a ground array sees some declinations far more than others, so an isotropic sky still looks uneven in its data
terms.excludes: the number of events, which is exposure times the true flux

terms.definition: a control sky made by keeping each event's declination and giving it a random right ascension; the Earth's rotation makes a ground array's exposure nearly even in right ascension, so the scramble keeps the exposure and removes any pattern
terms.excludes: a fully random sky, which would ignore the detector's exposure

terms.definition: a rule that raises a set of p values to control the expected share of false discoveries among the tests called significant; the smallest raw p is multiplied by the number of tests and larger ones by less
terms.excludes: an uncorrected p value read on its own when several tests were run

terms.definition: the share of planted skies, each with a pattern of known strength, in which the search finds the pattern at its preregistered threshold
terms.excludes: the chance that a pattern exists in the real sky

terms.field: metrology (the standard uncertainty of the GUM) and physics data tables
terms.definition: the plus-or-minus a table prints beside a value, meant as one standard deviation of the value's error; for a normal error the interval of one sigma either side holds the truth 68.27 percent of the time and two sigma 95.45 percent
terms.excludes: an expanded uncertainty already multiplied by a coverage factor, and any bound meant to hold always

terms.definition: the share of cases in which an interval drawn round an earlier value contains the value that later replaced it; here the interval is one or two of the earlier value's own stated sigma either side
terms.excludes: the share of intervals that contain the true value, which no later table can supply

terms.term: shift in units of the earlier sigma
terms.field: statistics, our usage; called a normalised residual in metrology
terms.definition: the size of the change in a quantity's value between an earlier and a later edition of a table, divided by the uncertainty stated in the earlier edition
terms.excludes: the sign of the change, and any uncertainty in the later value

terms.field: metrology, our usage; a coverage factor fitted after the fact
terms.definition: the multiple of the stated sigma that would have covered 68.27 or 95.45 percent of the later values; it is the matching percentile of the shifts in units of the earlier sigma, written k68 and k95
terms.excludes: a factor known before the later values were published

terms.term: Student t distribution and its tail index nu
terms.definition: a bell-shaped family with heavier tails than the normal curve; its degrees of freedom nu set the tail weight, so small nu means large shifts are common, nu of 1 is the Cauchy distribution and nu without limit is the normal curve
terms.excludes: skewed or bounded shapes

terms.definition: the Student t distribution with nu equal to 1, whose tails are so heavy that its mean and variance do not exist
terms.excludes: any distribution with a finite variance

terms.definition: the same coverage count repeated after dropping every quantity whose value did not change between the two editions, since an unchanged value counts as covered whatever its stated uncertainty
terms.excludes: a test of whether the unchanged values were right

terms.definition: a value fixed in advance and used in place of the unknown true value where no later edition settles it; here three values of the Hubble constant, 67.4, 70 and 73 km/s/Mpc, each reported on its own
terms.excludes: a claim that any of the three is the true value

terms.definition: measurements or derived values that feed both an earlier and a later edition of a table, so that the two editions are not independent and agree more than independent work would
terms.excludes: measurements made only for the later edition

terms.definition: redrawing the quantities of a table with replacement, here 300 times, and recomputing the coverage each time; the middle 95 percent of the recomputed values is the interval
terms.excludes: uncertainty from the choice of editions or from shared inputs, which resampling quantities does not touch

terms.definition: simulated shifts drawn from a standard normal distribution at the PDG sample size, so that every stated sigma is exactly right, scored the same way as the real shifts
terms.excludes: heavy tails and shared inputs

terms.definition: the average number of binary digits needed to write down each letter of a text under a given model of the text; one bit halves the number of equally likely choices, so 4.75 bits per letter is the cost of picking blindly among 27 symbols
terms.excludes: a count of bytes in a file, and any statement about meaning

terms.definition: the uncertainty of the next letter when the N minus 1 letters before it are known, averaged over the text; Shannon wrote it F with a subscript N, so F1 uses single-letter counts, F2 one letter of context and F3 two
terms.excludes: the entropy of the language as a whole, which is the limit as N grows

terms.definition: an entropy computed by putting the observed relative frequencies of a sample straight into the entropy formula, with no correction for the size of the sample
terms.excludes: corrected estimators that add a term for unseen or rare events

terms.field: data compression and statistical language modelling
terms.definition: a model that predicts the next symbol from counts of what followed the same few preceding symbols in training text, blending long and short contexts; prediction by partial matching (PPM) is the classic form
terms.excludes: models that use word meaning, grammar or knowledge outside the letter counts

terms.field: information theory and machine learning; also called cross-entropy
terms.definition: the average of minus the base-2 logarithm of the probability a model gave to the letter that came next, in bits per letter; it is the length of the code an ideal coder driven by the model would write
terms.excludes: the share of letters guessed right, and the entropy of the text itself, which log loss can only bound from above

terms.definition: text kept apart from the text a model was trained on and used only to score it
terms.excludes: any text whose counts entered the model

terms.definition: a reader guesses the next letter in order of preference until right; the share of letters found at the first, second and later guesses gives an upper and a lower bound on the entropy
terms.excludes: a direct measure of the probabilities a reader holds

terms.definition: a random text in which each symbol depends only on the two symbols before it, through a fixed table of probabilities, so its entropy per symbol can be computed exactly
terms.excludes: real text, whose dependence reaches further back

terms.definition: the observation that the frequency of a word falls roughly in inverse proportion to its rank in the frequency list
terms.excludes: an exact law that holds for every word or every text

terms.field: our usage, from machine learning practice on domain shift
terms.definition: the extra log loss a reader pays on another kind of text compared with a reader trained on that kind of text, both scored on the same held-out passage
terms.excludes: the difference in difficulty between two texts read by their own readers

terms.definition: the length of a compressed text in bits divided by the number of characters in the original; lower is better, and 8 is the cost of plain one-byte text
terms.excludes: bits per token or per byte, which divide by a different count

terms.definition: a method that turns a model's probability for each next symbol into a single binary number, so a symbol given probability p costs close to minus log2 p bits, and a decoder with the same model recovers the text exactly
terms.excludes: codes that give each symbol a fixed whole number of bits, such as Huffman codes

terms.definition: the sum over a text of minus log2 of the probability the model gave to each symbol that came next; a real arithmetic coder comes within a few bits of it
terms.excludes: a measured file size, and any cost of storing the model

terms.definition: prediction by partial matching, a compressor that predicts each character from counts of what followed the same preceding characters, falling back to shorter contexts when a longer one has not been seen; here method C with exclusion and contexts of up to 5 characters
terms.excludes: models with learned weights, such as neural language models

terms.definition: a general-purpose file compressor using the LZMA method, which replaces repeated strings with references to earlier copies; here at its strongest preset
terms.excludes: any model of language beyond repeated byte strings

terms.definition: the unit a language model reads and predicts, a whole word, part of a word or a single character taken from a fixed vocabulary of tens of thousands of pieces
terms.excludes: a character or a byte

terms.field: machine learning; in evaluation also called training-data contamination
terms.definition: a model's ability to predict a specific text because that text, or close copies of it, was in its training data, as distinct from predicting text of the same kind it has not seen
terms.excludes: any claim about how the model stores the text internally

terms.definition: a control added after the first results were seen; it can test an explanation but carries less weight than a control fixed in advance, because the choice of control could follow the result
terms.excludes: controls named in the preregistration

terms.field: our usage, after the two-part code of minimum description length
terms.definition: the number of characters a model must compress before the bits it saves over another compressor add up to the size of the model itself, when the model has to be sent along with the message
terms.excludes: a compression ratio on one text, which ignores the cost of the model

terms.definition: a test of a method on a case where the true answer is fixed by physics or by construction, so that any wrong reading is a fault of the method
terms.excludes: agreement with another method, which can share the same fault

terms.definition: a regression test of whether the past values of one series improve the prediction of another beyond that series' own past; here an F test on lags 1 and 2
terms.excludes: a test of same-year effects, and proof of a physical cause

terms.definition: a set of units, here tree-ring sites, each observed over time and analysed together so that one statistic summarises all of them
terms.excludes: a verdict reached site by site, and a pooled regression that treats all years of all sites as one series

terms.definition: the mean over sites of d, the z-score of the climate-to-ring Granger test minus that of the ring-to-climate test; positive values point from summer temperature to ring width
terms.excludes: a test of significance at any one site

terms.definition: the point of the standard normal distribution that leaves the p value above it, so that a smaller p gives a larger z; here capped at 6
terms.excludes: a standardised value of the data themselves

terms.definition: a filter that keeps fast variation and removes slow trends; here each series minus a Gaussian smooth of width 10 years, then scaled to unit variance
terms.excludes: first differences, which are reported as a separate arm

terms.definition: each year's value minus the previous year's, a second way to remove slow trends that weights the fastest changes most
terms.excludes: the high-pass filter, which removes trends by smoothing

terms.definition: a copy of a series built by repeated rounds of Fourier phase randomisation and rank reordering, so that it keeps both the original spectrum, and with it the autocorrelation, and the original set of values, while its timing against any other series is lost
terms.excludes: a shuffle of single years, which destroys the autocorrelation

terms.definition: the share of sites at which the Granger test in one direction gives p 0.05 or below; for synthetic worlds it is averaged over the draws
terms.excludes: a rate corrected for testing 161 sites

terms.definition: the share of sites at which the sign of d matches the direction planted in a synthetic world; 0.5 is what a coin would give
terms.excludes: whether the test at any site is significant

terms.definition: an interval made by resampling whole 2 degree blocks of sites with replacement, here 2,000 times, so that neighbouring sites that share climate move together and the interval is not too narrow
terms.excludes: a bootstrap over single sites, and a binomial interval that treats sites as independent

terms.definition: a control in which each ring series is paired with the summer temperature of a random site at least 1,000 km away, so that real coupling is removed while both series keep their own form; repeated 199 times
terms.excludes: pairings with nearby sites, which share regional climate

terms.definition: the same test run on both series read backwards in time; a method that reads direction from lag order should flip
terms.excludes: a control on coupling strength

terms.definition: a preregistered rule on a synthetic world that the instrument must pass before any reading of the real data counts; under the kill condition a single failure removes all standing
terms.excludes: power checks and limit checks, which were recorded but could not remove standing

terms.definition: a rule that adjusts a set of p values so that, among the tests called significant, the expected share of false calls stays at or below a chosen rate, here 0.05; the adjusted value is called q
terms.excludes: the stricter Bonferroni rule, which bounds the chance of any false call

terms.definition: the slope on the previous year's summer temperature in a regression of this year's ring width on this year's and last year's summer temperature
terms.excludes: the same-year slope, and any effect of the ring's own past unless it is added to the regression
